questions.question: What are Spring bean scopes? How do singleton, prototype, request, and session differ?
questions.title: Bean Scopes: Singleton vs Prototype vs Request vs Session
questions.direct_answer: Spring scopes control how many instances of a bean exist and for how long. Singleton (the default) creates one shared instance per container. Prototype creates a new instance on every injection or getBean() call. Request and Session scopes (available in web contexts) create one instance per HTTP request or session respectively.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of scope selection and awareness of the 'scoped proxy' problem when injecting a short-lived bean into a singleton.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming singleton means thread-safe, or not knowing that Spring does NOT manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans after creation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the scoped-proxy pattern (@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)) needed when injecting a request/session-scoped bean into a singleton.

sections.title: Why Singleton Doesn't Mean Thread-Safe — and Why Prototype Doesn't Mean Disposable
sections.content:
Spring's default scope is **singleton** — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared by every injection point. Most developers stop there and never think about scope again. But there are two misconceptions that cause real bugs.

First, **singleton does not mean thread-safe**. Spring creates one instance and hands the same reference to every thread. If that bean has mutable state — a field that changes between requests — every concurrent request sees and modifies the same field. Race conditions are invisible until they produce corrupted data in production.

Second, **prototype scope means Spring creates a new instance every time the bean is requested** — but Spring does not manage the full lifecycle. There's no `@PreDestroy` call, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean opens a database connection, Spring won't close it. Cleanup is your responsibility.

The web scopes — `request` and `session` — exist specifically for stateful web interactions where the state must be isolated per HTTP request or per user session. But injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton creates a subtle problem that requires **scoped proxies** to solve.

sections.title: Five Scopes, Two Lifecycles: What Spring Manages and What It Doesn't
sections.content:
The critical distinction isn't just 'how many instances' — it's what **lifecycle callbacks Spring guarantees** for each scope. Singleton beans get full lifecycle management including destruction. Prototype beans get creation only.

| Scope | Instances | Lifetime | Thread-safe? | @PreDestroy called? | Web required? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| singleton | 1 per container | Application lifetime | ⚠️ Not inherently | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| prototype | 1 per injection/getBean | Until GC | ✅ Yes (isolated) | ❌ No | ❌ No |
| request | 1 per HTTP request | HTTP request | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| session | 1 per HTTP session | HTTP session | ⚠️ Same user, different threads | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| application | 1 per ServletContext | App lifetime | ⚠️ Same as singleton | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| websocket | 1 per WebSocket session | WS session | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |

sections.title: The Scoped Proxy Problem: Why Request-Scoped Beans Break in Singletons
Custom Scopes, Scope Proxying Internals, and Production Patterns
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton does not mean thread-safe** — Spring creates one shared instance and gives the same reference to every thread; mutable state in a singleton bean is a race condition.
- **Prototype: Spring creates but never destroys** — Spring instantiates a new prototype on every injection or `getBean()` call but never calls `@PreDestroy`; resources must be closed by the calling code.
- **Scoped proxy required for request/session beans in singletons** — a singleton is created at startup before any HTTP request exists; `@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` injects a CGLIB proxy that resolves the actual bean per-request at call time.
- **`BeanCreationException: no thread-bound request found`** — the startup error when a request-scoped bean is injected into a singleton without `proxyMode`.
- **`@Scope("prototype")` + `ObjectProvider<T>` for fresh instances in singletons** — injecting a prototype directly into a singleton produces one shared instance; `ObjectProvider.getObject()` creates a fresh prototype on every call.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's default scope is singleton — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared across all threads. Most developers never change this and assume it means safe. Two misconceptions cause real bugs.

**Singleton**
- One instance per container, shared across all threads — mutable state in a singleton bean is a race condition waiting to happen
- Full lifecycle: Spring calls `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy`; the bean lives for the entire application lifetime

**Prototype**
- New instance every time the bean is injected or `getBean()` is called — isolated, no sharing between threads
- Spring creates but never destroys prototype beans; `@PreDestroy` is never called; if the prototype holds a database connection or file handle, the calling code must close it

**Request and Session scopes**
- One instance per HTTP request or per HTTP session — correct for per-user or per-request state
- Injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton is the most common scope trap: the singleton is created at startup before any request exists; Spring throws `BeanCreationException: no thread-bound request found`
- Fix: `@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` — Spring injects a CGLIB proxy; each method call resolves the real request-scoped bean from the current thread

Use singleton for stateless services (the default), prototype when you need isolated mutable state per use, request/session for web-specific state. Never store per-request state in a singleton field.

questions.title: Prototype Bean in Singleton — The Scoping Trap
questions.question: What happens when you inject a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton bean?

sections.title: The Injection That Happens Once When You Expected It to Happen Every Time
sections.content:
Injecting a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton is one of Spring's most common traps. The developer expects a **fresh instance** on every use — that's why they chose prototype scope. But Spring injects the prototype once during the singleton's construction, and the singleton holds that same instance forever. The prototype becomes a de facto singleton, defeating the entire purpose of prototype scope.

The root cause is a scope mismatch. Singleton beans are created once and their dependencies are injected once. When a prototype bean is declared as a constructor or field dependency of a singleton, Spring resolves it during singleton creation, creates one prototype instance, and injects it. From that point on, the singleton holds a fixed reference. No mechanism exists to "re-inject" the field later.

This manifests as a concurrency bug or a state leak. A prototype bean is typically used because it holds per-use state — a request tracker, a parser with internal buffers, a computation context. When it's shared across threads via a singleton, that per-use state is corrupted. Two concurrent requests write to the same object, and the output is a mixture of both requests' data.

The fix is to avoid holding a prototype as a field entirely. Instead, ask Spring for a new instance each time you need one. Spring provides three mechanisms for this: `ObjectProvider<T>`, `ObjectFactory<T>`, and `@Lookup` method injection. `ObjectProvider` is the recommended approach because it's type-safe, well-documented, and doesn't require CGLIB subclassing.

The bug manifests differently depending on whether the singleton is used by a single thread or many. In single-threaded scenarios (like a command-line batch application), the singleton reuses the same prototype instance on every invocation — state accumulates from previous runs. In multi-threaded web applications, concurrent requests share the prototype's mutable state, producing data corruption that appears intermittently and is nearly impossible to reproduce in isolation.

sections.title: ObjectProvider: The Clean Fix for Scope Mismatch
Three Solutions to Scope Mismatch — And Why Each Has Different Trade-offs
sections.content:
When a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, the prototype's state is shared across all uses of the singleton — defeating the purpose of prototype scope. Spring provides three solutions, each with different trade-offs.

**`ObjectProvider<T>` (recommended):** Inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a new instance. The provider is singleton-scoped, but each `getObject()` call creates a new prototype instance. This is the cleanest solution — no AOP proxy, no container coupling, testable without Spring.

**Scoped proxy (`@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)`):** Spring wraps the prototype bean in a CGLIB proxy. Every call through the proxy creates a new prototype instance. The singleton receives the proxy instead of a real instance — from its perspective, the dependency is 'always there', but the proxy creates fresh instances per call. This works transparently but requires CGLIB bytecode manipulation and adds complexity visible in debugging sessions (stack traces show proxy classes).

**`ApplicationContext.getBean()`:** Call `getBean(PrototypeBean.class)` each time you need an instance. This works but couples your class to the Spring container — a `BeanFactory` dependency in business logic is a code smell. It's acceptable in infrastructure code (factories, adapters) where Spring dependency is already explicit.

For **thread-safe stateful beans**, consider whether prototype scope is actually the right solution. If the state is request-specific, request scope (`@Scope("request")`) in a web application may be more appropriate. If the state is conversation-specific (multi-step flow), session scope makes more sense. Prototype is correct when each calling component needs a truly independent instance with independent mutable state.

A design-level question worth asking before reaching for prototype scope: **does this bean need to be a Spring bean at all?** If the only reason it's a Spring bean is that it has dependencies, but you want a fresh instance every time, consider a factory bean or builder pattern that creates new instances directly. A factory method annotated `@Bean @Scope("prototype")` works, but sometimes `new MyObject(injectedDep)` with the dependency constructor-injected into the factory is cleaner. Prototype scope adds complexity that's only justified when the bean itself needs the full Spring lifecycle — `@PostConstruct`, AOP wrapping, `@Autowired` dependencies on the prototype itself.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prototype injected into singleton becomes a singleton** — Spring injects the prototype exactly once during singleton construction; the singleton holds that same instance forever, defeating prototype scope.
- **`ObjectProvider<T>` is the clean fix** — inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a fresh instance; the provider is singleton-scoped, creation happens at call time.
- **`ApplicationContext.getBean()` works but is a code smell** — coupling business logic to the Spring API is an anti-pattern; use `ObjectProvider` or `@Lookup` instead.
- **`@Lookup` method injection uses CGLIB** — Spring subclasses the singleton and overrides the annotated abstract method to return a new prototype instance; no field, no provider dependency, but requires CGLIB subclassing.
- **Spring never calls `@PreDestroy` on prototype instances** — resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility regardless of how the prototype was obtained.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Injecting a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton is one of Spring's most common traps. The developer expects a fresh instance on every use — that's why they chose prototype. But Spring injects the prototype exactly once during the singleton's construction and never again. The prototype becomes a de facto singleton.

**Why it happens**
- Singleton beans are created once and their dependencies are injected once
- When a prototype is a constructor or field dependency of a singleton, Spring resolves it at singleton creation time — one prototype instance, held forever
- Two concurrent requests share the prototype's mutable state — data corruption that appears intermittently

**The fix: `ObjectProvider`**
- Inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` instead of the bean itself — the provider is singleton-scoped
- Call `.getObject()` each time you need a fresh instance — Spring creates a new prototype on every call
- Cleaner than `ApplicationContext.getBean()`, which couples business code to the Spring API

**The `@Lookup` alternative**
- Annotate an abstract method with `@Lookup` — Spring CGLIB-subclasses the singleton and overrides the method to return a new prototype instance on every call

Spring never calls `@PreDestroy` on prototype beans, regardless of how they were obtained. If the prototype holds resources, the calling code owns cleanup.

questions.question: Can you walk me through the complete Spring Bean lifecycle from instantiation to destruction?
questions.title: Spring Bean Lifecycle
questions.direct_answer: A Spring bean goes through a well-defined sequence: the container instantiates it, injects dependencies, calls post-construction callbacks like @PostConstruct, makes it available for use, and finally calls @PreDestroy before removing it from context. Understanding this order is critical when you need to set up resources after injection or release them cleanly on shutdown.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the container's role and can reason about ordering bugs (e.g., using a dependency before injection is complete).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing @PostConstruct with the constructor, or not knowing that InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet runs before @PostConstruct.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention BeanPostProcessor hooks (postProcessBeforeInitialization / postProcessAfterInitialization) and how they power AOP proxying.

sections.title: Why the Order of Six Lifecycle Phases Matters — and Where Most Bugs Hide
sections.content:
The Spring IoC container manages each bean through a precise lifecycle. Hooks are provided at every stage so you can plug in custom logic — from property overrides to proxy wrapping to resource cleanup.

The Spring Bean lifecycle is a precisely ordered sequence of callbacks that gives developers hooks at every critical transition. Understanding it demonstrates senior-level Spring knowledge.

**Phase 1 — Instantiation:** The container uses the bean's constructor (or a factory method) to create the raw Java object. At this point, no dependencies have been injected — fields are null. If constructor injection is used, dependencies are resolved and provided as constructor arguments during this phase.

**Phase 2 — Dependency Injection:** After instantiation, Spring injects dependencies via setter methods or field injection (`@Autowired`). The `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` handles `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject` annotations. If a required dependency cannot be resolved, the context fails to start.

**Phase 3 — Post-Construction Callbacks:** `@PostConstruct` methods (or `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`) run after all dependencies are injected. This is the safest place for initialization logic that depends on injected beans — connection pool warmup, cache population, or validation. `@PostConstruct` runs before `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization`.

**Phase 4 — BeanPostProcessor:** Spring iterates over all registered `BeanPostProcessor` implementations and calls `postProcessBeforeInitialization` and `postProcessAfterInitialization` on every bean. This is how AOP proxies are created (`AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator`), `@Scheduled` methods are registered, and `@Async` methods are wrapped. After this phase, the bean may be a proxy rather than the original object.

**Phase 5 — In Use:** The bean serves application requests. Singleton beans live for the entire application lifetime. Prototype beans are handed off and the container does not manage them further.

**Phase 6 — Destruction:** When the context shuts down, `@PreDestroy` methods (or `DisposableBean.destroy()`) run on singleton beans. This is where you close connections, flush caches, and release external resources. Prototype beans do not receive destruction callbacks because the container does not track them.

sections.title: Instantiation and Injection: Where Constructor Code Can't See @Autowired Fields
Post-Construction Callbacks: @PostConstruct vs InitializingBean vs @Bean(initMethod)
sections.content:
After injection completes, Spring fires **initialization callbacks** in a specific order. If a bean implements multiple callback mechanisms, they execute in this sequence: `@PostConstruct` first, then `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`, then the custom `initMethod` declared in `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")`.

**`@PostConstruct`** is the modern standard — a JSR-250 annotation that marks a method to run once after all dependencies are injected. It's clean, framework-agnostic (works outside Spring), and clearly communicates intent. Use it for connection pool warm-up, cache preloading, or any setup that requires injected collaborators.

**`InitializingBean`** is Spring's older interface approach. Implementing `afterPropertiesSet()` couples your class to the Spring API, which makes it harder to reuse outside the container. It still appears in Spring's own codebase and in legacy applications but is not recommended for new code.

**`@Bean(initMethod = "setup")`** is useful when you don't control the class source — third-party libraries whose beans need initialization. You specify the method name as a string in the `@Bean` declaration, and Spring calls it via reflection after injection.

A practical rule: use `@PostConstruct` for your own classes, `initMethod` for third-party classes, and avoid `InitializingBean` unless you're extending Spring's own framework code.

sections.title: BeanPostProcessor: The Hook That Creates Proxies for @Transactional and @Cacheable
sections.content:
After initialization callbacks complete, Spring invokes `BeanPostProcessor` implementations. These are the most powerful lifecycle extension point — they can inspect, modify, or **replace** the bean entirely.

The `BeanPostProcessor` interface defines two methods: `postProcessBeforeInitialization(bean, name)` runs before `@PostConstruct`, and `postProcessAfterInitialization(bean, name)` runs after. The 'after' hook is where **proxy creation** happens.

When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring's `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` — a `BeanPostProcessor` — detects it during the 'after' phase. Instead of returning the original bean, it returns a **CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy** that wraps the original. Every external call to the bean goes through the proxy, which manages the transaction lifecycle.

This is why **self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional`**. When a method inside the bean calls another method on `this`, it bypasses the proxy and hits the original object directly — no transaction management, no caching, no aspect. The proxy only intercepts calls that come through the injected reference.

The same mechanism powers `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, `@Retry`, and every other annotation-driven aspect in Spring. Understanding that these work through post-processing proxies explains most of the 'why doesn't my annotation work?' debugging scenarios.

sections.title: Destruction: @PreDestroy Runs for Singletons But Not for Prototypes
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Autowired` fields are null in the constructor** — field injection fires in `postProcessProperties` after construction, not during; use constructor injection or move initialization to `@PostConstruct`.
- **Initialization callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when a bean implements multiple mechanisms, they fire in this sequence; `@PostConstruct` always runs first.
- **`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization` creates proxies** — `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the original bean with a CGLIB proxy here; what other beans inject may be a proxy, not the original class.
- **`@PreDestroy` is never called on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility.
- **`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies bean definitions; `BeanPostProcessor` modifies bean instances** — `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`; `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is a `BeanPostProcessor`.
- **Destruction runs in reverse creation order** — singletons are destroyed before the beans they depend on, guaranteeing clean shutdown sequencing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Spring bean lifecycle is a precisely ordered sequence of phases. Every annotation-driven feature — `@Autowired`, `@PostConstruct`, `@Transactional`, `@PreDestroy` — fires at a specific point in that sequence. Knowing the order explains the bugs.

**Instantiation and injection**
- Constructor injection: dependencies are resolved first, then the constructor runs — the object is fully wired from line one
- Field/setter injection: the constructor runs first (no-arg), then `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` fires in `postProcessProperties` — `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor body

**Initialization callbacks — in this order**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — the safe place for startup logic that depends on injected collaborators
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach, avoid in new code
- `@Bean(initMethod)` fires last — for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**`BeanPostProcessor` — where proxies are created**
- `postProcessAfterInitialization` runs after all callbacks; it can return a different object
- This is how `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the bean with a CGLIB proxy
- Self-invocation via `this` bypasses the proxy — which is why `@Transactional` on an internal call does not work

**Destruction**
- `@PreDestroy` runs on singletons in reverse creation order when the context shuts down
- Prototype beans are handed off and never get `@PreDestroy` — Spring cannot call what it does not track

questions.question: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy — Bean Initialization and Destruction Callbacks
questions.title: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy — Bean Initialization and Destruction Callbacks

sections.title: Why You Can't Use @Autowired Fields in the Constructor — and What @PostConstruct Fixes
sections.content:
The problem `@PostConstruct` solves is a **timing gap** in the bean lifecycle. When Spring creates a bean, the constructor runs first. If the bean uses field injection, `@Autowired` fields are `null` during the constructor — they haven't been injected yet. Any initialization logic that depends on injected collaborators fails with `NullPointerException`.

`@PostConstruct` marks a method that Spring calls **after dependency injection is complete** but before the bean is put into service. It's the safe place for startup logic: warming caches, validating configuration, opening connections, or registering listeners.

`@PreDestroy` is the mirror — it runs when the `ApplicationContext` shuts down, giving the bean a chance to release resources cleanly. Close connection pools, flush buffers, deregister from external services. Together, these two annotations cover the **initialization and cleanup** that constructors and finalizers can't handle reliably.

The important caveat is scope. **`@PreDestroy` only runs for singleton beans.** Spring doesn't track prototype instances after creation — there's no shutdown hook, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean acquires resources, the calling code must close them explicitly.

sections.title: The Callback Order: @PostConstruct → InitializingBean → initMethod
@PreDestroy and Graceful Shutdown: What Gets Cleaned Up and What Doesn't
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PostConstruct` is the safe place for initialization** — all `@Autowired` dependencies are fully injected when it runs; the constructor is not safe for field-injected deps.
- **Callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when multiple mechanisms exist on one bean, they fire in this sequence.
- **`@PreDestroy` never fires on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; switching a singleton to prototype without adding explicit cleanup causes resource leaks.
- **`@Bean(destroyMethod="")` prevents auto-detected cleanup** — Spring auto-infers `destroyMethod` as `close()` or `shutdown()` for `@Bean` methods; set it to empty string to disable if auto-detection causes problems.
- **`@PreDestroy` fires in reverse creation order** — singletons are destroyed before the singletons they depend on, guaranteeing clean shutdown sequencing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` exist because constructors and finalizers cannot reliably handle initialization and cleanup in a dependency-injected world.

**Why the constructor is not enough**
- With field injection, `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor — they have not been injected yet
- `@PostConstruct` runs after all injection is complete — it is the correct place to warm caches, validate configuration, open connections, or register listeners that depend on injected collaborators

**Callback order when all three exist on one bean**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — JSR-250 standard, works in any Jakarta EE container, not just Spring
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach; avoid in new code, it couples to the Spring API
- `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")` fires last — useful for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**`@PreDestroy` — cleanup on shutdown**
- Runs on singleton beans in reverse creation order when `ApplicationContext.close()` is called
- Never called on prototype beans — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation
- Switch a singleton to prototype scope without adding explicit cleanup and connections or threads leak silently

The practical rule: use `@PostConstruct` for your own classes, `@Bean(initMethod)` for third-party beans, and `@PreDestroy` to release any resource the bean acquired during initialization.

sections.title: Why Eager Initialization Is Usually Better — and When @Lazy Actually Helps
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is **eager initialization** — all singleton beans are created at startup, before the application handles any requests. This is deliberate: configuration errors, missing dependencies, and circular references surface immediately instead of blowing up on the first user request.

`@Lazy` changes this to **on-demand initialization** — the bean is created the first time it's actually needed. This sounds like an optimization, but it's a trade-off. You gain faster startup at the cost of **deferred failure detection**. A miswired `@Lazy` bean won't throw `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup — it'll throw it on the first request that triggers its creation.

The legitimate use cases for `@Lazy` are narrow: beans that are **expensive to create** and **not always needed** (a reporting engine that's only used on Sundays), beans involved in **circular dependency breaking** (a temporary fix, not a design solution), and beans that depend on **runtime state** not available at startup (request-scoped resources).

For most applications, the startup time saved by `@Lazy` is measured in milliseconds — not worth the risk of runtime failures.

sections.title: How @Lazy Works: The Proxy That Delays Creation Until First Use
The Circular Dependency Hack: Why @Lazy Masks a Design Problem
sections.content:
The most common use of `@Lazy` in production codebases is **breaking circular dependencies**. When `ServiceA` depends on `ServiceB` and `ServiceB` depends on `ServiceA`, constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. Adding `@Lazy` to one side creates a proxy that defers creation, breaking the cycle.

This works, but it's a **band-aid**. The circular dependency is a design smell — two classes that depend on each other usually share a responsibility that should be extracted into a third class, or the interaction should be decoupled through events or an interface.

The danger of `@Lazy` as a circular dependency fix is that it hides the problem. The code compiles, the tests pass, but the design issue remains. When someone later refactors one of the classes, the `@Lazy` annotation seems arbitrary and gets removed — resurfacing the original `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. At that point, nobody remembers why it was there.

**The proper fix** is to extract the shared concern, use `ApplicationEventPublisher` for decoupled communication, or restructure the dependency graph. Use `@Lazy` for circular dependencies only as a temporary workaround with a `// TODO: fix circular dependency` comment.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Lazy` defers creation but not failure detection** — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean does not fail at startup; it fails on the first request that triggers its creation — a production failure instead of a deployment failure.
- **Spring injects a CGLIB proxy, not the real bean** — when a dependency is `@Lazy`, the injection point receives a proxy; the real bean is created on the first proxy method call.
- **`@Lazy` as a circular dependency fix is a design smell** — it breaks the cycle by deferring one side but hides the SRP violation; the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns when someone removes the annotation during refactoring.
- **The legitimate use cases are narrow** — expensive beans only needed occasionally (reporting engines), beans with runtime-state dependencies not available at startup.
- **`@Lazy` on the injection point parameter, not the bean class** — parameter-level placement gives fine-grained control; one consumer gets a lazy proxy while another gets the real bean eagerly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is eager initialization — all singleton beans are created at startup before the application handles any request. This is deliberate: configuration errors surface immediately instead of crashing on the first user request. `@Lazy` trades that safety for faster startup.

**What it does**
- The bean definition is still registered — Spring knows it exists
- Instead of creating the bean at startup, Spring injects a CGLIB proxy into dependents
- The real bean is created on the first method call through the proxy

**The trade-off**
- Faster startup — the expensive bean is not created until needed
- Deferred failure detection — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean will not fail startup; it fails on the first request that triggers it, which is a production failure instead of a deployment failure

**The circular dependency trap**
- The most common use of `@Lazy` in production is breaking circular dependencies — adding it to one side creates a proxy that defers creation, breaking the cycle
- This masks the design problem; when someone removes the annotation during refactoring, the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns with no explanation of why it was there
- Fix the design instead: extract the shared concern, use events, or apply interface segregation

Use `@Lazy` for genuinely expensive beans that are not always needed. Use it at the injection point parameter level for fine-grained control. Never use it as a permanent fix for circular dependencies.

sections.title: Why Circular Dependencies Are a Design Problem, Not a Framework Problem
sections.content:
A circular dependency means `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` to be created, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` to be created — a deadlock that Spring can't resolve for constructor injection. The temptation is to find a framework workaround (`@Lazy`, setter injection). The correct response is to **fix the design**.

Circular dependencies almost always signal a **Single Responsibility violation** — two classes that share a concern which should be extracted into a third class. Or they signal **missing abstraction** — the classes should communicate through events or an interface instead of direct references.

Spring's behavior depends on the injection style. **Constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup** — fast and visible. Field and setter injection resolve the cycle silently using early references (Spring injects a partially-constructed bean), which can produce subtle runtime bugs when the partially-constructed bean is used before its dependencies are fully wired.

Spring Boot 2.6+ made this stricter by **disabling circular dependency resolution by default**. Even field-injected cycles now throw at startup unless you explicitly opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`. This change reflects the community consensus that circular dependencies should be fixed, not tolerated.

sections.title: The BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: How to Read the Stack Trace
sections.content:
When Spring detects a circular dependency with constructor injection, the error message names the beans involved. The typical message looks like: 'Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?'

The stack trace shows the dependency chain: Spring tries to create `ServiceA`, which requires `ServiceB`, which requires `ServiceA` — and `ServiceA` is already being created. The chain can be longer: A → B → C → A.

The fix starts with **understanding why both classes need each other**. Usually one of these patterns is the root cause:

**Pattern 1: Shared responsibility.** `OrderService` calls `InventoryService.reserve()`, and `InventoryService` calls `OrderService.getOrder()`. Both services handle order-related logic — extract an `OrderRepository` that both depend on instead of depending on each other.

**Pattern 2: Event-worthy interaction.** `PaymentService` notifies `NotificationService` of a payment, and `NotificationService` queries `PaymentService` for details. Replace the direct call with an `ApplicationEvent` — `PaymentService` publishes a `PaymentCompleted` event, and `NotificationService` listens for it. No mutual dependency.

sections.title: Three Fixes: Extract, Event, Interface — and Why @Lazy Is the Wrong Answer
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Constructor injection fails fast; field injection used to hide cycles** — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup for constructor cycles; Spring Boot 2.6+ blocks field/setter injection cycles by default too.
- **`spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` is the escape hatch, not the fix** — enabling it acknowledges the design problem and defers it; the community consensus is to eliminate circular dependencies, not tolerate them.
- **Root cause is almost always SRP violation** — two classes that depend on each other share logic that belongs in a third class.
- **Fix 1: extract the shared concern** — create class C that both A and B depend on instead of depending on each other.
- **Fix 2: replace one direction with events** — `ApplicationEventPublisher` breaks the mutual dependency; A publishes, B listens, one-way dependency remains.
- **`@Lazy` breaks the cycle but hides the problem** — use only as a temporary workaround with a comment explaining why; it causes `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` to resurface when someone removes it during refactoring.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A circular dependency means `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` to be created, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` — a deadlock. Spring's response depends on the injection style, and the difference matters.

**Constructor injection**
- Spring detects the deadlock immediately and throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup — a clear failure message naming all beans in the cycle
- Spring Boot 2.6+ extended this to field and setter injection by default — even those cycles now fail at startup unless you opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`

**Why it is a design problem**
- Circular dependencies almost always signal that two classes share a responsibility that belongs in a third class
- Or they signal direct coupling where events should decouple the interaction

**The three proper fixes**
- Extract the shared concern into a class C — both A and B depend on C, not on each other
- Replace one direction with `ApplicationEventPublisher` — A publishes an event, B listens; one-way dependency remains, the cycle is gone
- Interface segregation — if B only needs one method from A, extract it into a narrow interface; B depends on the interface, not on all of A

`@Lazy` breaks the cycle by deferring one side but hides the design problem entirely. When someone removes the annotation during refactoring, the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns with no explanation of why it was there. Use `@Lazy` only as a temporary workaround.
